name: Familiarisation
description: Two checks in the hangar. Neither decides who gets which machine -- that is a conversation between players, not a roll. What these decide is how much a first acquaintance gives back, and whether anybody finds the thing at the far end.

dc.basis: level 1 standard DC 15. Not pass-fail -- this decides how much the machine gives back on a first acquaintance, and every result gets them in the seat

outcomes.criticalSuccess: They find the previous pilot's left-behind thing without looking for it, work out one control that is not labelled, and get a genuine feel for the machine. Treat them as comfortable in it from the first minute of the exercise.
outcomes.success: The seat, the smell, the reach of the controls, and the thing a previous pilot left behind.
outcomes.failure: It is bigger inside than it looked and nothing is where a person would put it. They are in, and nothing is broken, and the seat was built for somebody with a longer reach.
outcomes.criticalFailure: As failure, and something gets grabbed that should not have been grabbed. A klaxon, a floodlight, or the grapple arm swinging ten feet. No damage, considerable noise, and the whole hangar looks round.

bySkill.crafting: Reading the machine as a machine -- what has been repaired, what has been bodged, what the previous pilot cared about.
bySkill.perception: The small stuff: the tin, the photograph, the tally by the door, the wear on one pedal and not the other.
bySkill.athletics: Getting properly settled and finding the reach of everything, which on a machine built for an adult is a real question.
bySkill.survival: What this thing would be like to spend eleven hours in, which is the question that actually matters later.

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step easy. Nothing is being hidden -- the difficulty is only in thinking to look, and anybody who asks Hulda directly is simply told

outcomes.criticalSuccess: The helicopter, airworthy, and the whole truth about it: nobody on this base is currently rated to fly one, the rating is a real course that costs real quarters, and Hulda will sign the paperwork the day somebody qualifies.
outcomes.success: A helicopter, under dust sheets, in working order, not on the chalk board.
outcomes.failure: Screens, dust sheets, and something large behind them. Asking anybody gets a straight answer, so this is barely a failure at all.
outcomes.criticalFailure: As failure, and they knock a screen over doing it. Noise, no harm, and Hulda is delighted rather than annoyed.

participants: Individually -- each pilot meets their own machine
notes:
NO ROLL DECIDES WHO GETS WHICH MACHINE. If two players want the same one, that is a conversation between those two players and it belongs to them. Hulda Brack will not adjudicate it and says so.

THE HELICOPTER IS NOT A TEASE. There is a real route to it, it is stated plainly on any success, and the door is open. A long-term want with a known price is a gift to a player; a locked box is not.

THE CRITICAL FAILURE IN THE CAB IS COMEDY, NOT DAMAGE. Nothing breaks, nobody is hurt, and no machine is withheld as a result. The entire hangar looking round is the whole cost.

PRICING AN INVENTED APPROACH. Standard Chapter One ladder: DC 13 if it costs them something real, DC 15 for the obvious way, DC 17 if it is free or skips a step, DC 20 if it would get more than the scene was going to give.
